leaders.notes: Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College, which the Little Rock Board of Education created in 1927 and operated as a school-district institution. Hall held the college presidency while serving as Little Rock School District superintendent (1909-1941); Hall High School is named for him.

Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College. Larson, a Swedish-born high school principal, urged the Little Rock Board of Education to found LRJC in 1927 and is regarded as its founder; he resigned the Central High School principalship to devote himself to the college and died in office in 1949. The UA Little Rock official list gives 1930-1949; the Encyclopedia of Arkansas photo caption dates his presidency from 1929 and the UA Little Rock history page says 1930-1950.

Title in effect: President of Little Rock Junior College. Published as Granville D. Davis by the Encyclopedia of Arkansas, which notes he was a member of the first LRJC graduating class, making him an alumnus-president. His immediately prior and subsequent positions could not be verified from available sources.

Title in effect: acting president of Little Rock Junior College, as published on the university's official list of past presidents and chancellors. He bridged the two years between Granville Davis and Carey V. Stabler; no verifiable record of his prior or subsequent positions was found.

leaders.notes: Title in effect: President. Under Stabler, Little Rock Junior College became the independent, private, four-year Little Rock University in fall 1957, and course offerings grew from roughly 80 in 1956 to about 500 by 1967. He continued in office when the institution joined the University of Arkansas System in 1969, at which point his title changed from president to chancellor. His position immediately before 1956 could not be verified.

leaders.priorInstitution: Little Rock University (the same institution, before its 1969 merger into the UA System)
leaders.notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. Same person as the preceding entry, listed separately by the university because the 1969 merger of Little Rock University into the University of Arkansas System converted the office from president to chancellor. He resigned in 1972; Stabler Hall is named for him. What he did after resigning could not be verified.

leaders.notes: Title in effect: acting chancellor. Fribourgh, a biologist, joined Little Rock Junior College in 1949 and spent 45 years at the institution through its Little Rock University and UALR eras, serving as chief academic officer from 1969 to 1984 and stepping up as acting chancellor after Stabler's resignation. Fribourgh Hall and the university's Fribourgh Award are named for him; he died March 6, 2014.

leaders.nextRole: President and Professor of Education and Psychology
leaders.notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire, Ross accepted the UALR chancellorship in January 1973 as chancellor and professor of education and psychology, and is credited with establishing UALR's autonomy within the UA System, growing degree programs from 28 to 73 and enrollment from about 3,500 to 9,652. He left in summer 1982, was named president of Western Washington University in January 1983, and was killed in a plane crash in November 1987 along with two WWU vice presidents and the pilot. He was also a past president of ACPA.

Title in effect: Chancellor. Young emphasized a traditional liberal arts direction, established campus-wide learning goals, and opened UALR's first residential dormitory. His position immediately before 1982 and his destination after leaving in 1992 could not be verified from available sources; the University of Arkansas holds biographical materials on him in its archives.

leaders.notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire, Hathaway had chaired the physics department at Kansas State University for 16 years, then was dean of the College of Sciences and Engineering at the University of Texas at San Antonio (1981-1986) and vice president for academic affairs at Wright State University (1986-1993). As chancellor he returned UALR to an urban/metropolitan mission and created the Cyber College in 1998. He stayed on as a UALR faculty member after 2002 and died August 5, 2025, at age 89.

leaders.notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. A thoroughly internal appointment: Anderson joined UALR in 1971 as an assistant professor of political science, became founding dean of the graduate school in 1977 and provost in 1984, held the provostship for nearly two decades, and was named chancellor in 2003 after an earlier interim term. He served 13 years as chancellor and 45 years at the institution, oversaw the Donaghey College of Engineering, the Jack Stephens Center and three residence halls, and retired effective June 30, 2016; the Anderson Institute on Race and Ethnicity was named for him that year.

leaders.notes: Title in effect: interim chancellor. Named interim chancellor on June 28, 2016 upon Joel Anderson's June 30 retirement, she led the campus from July 1 to August 30, 2016, working closely with UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt until Andrew Rogerson began September 1. She was published as Zulma Toro-Ramos when hired as UALR provost in 2012, and in October 2016 was selected as the thirteenth president of Central Connecticut State University, taking office January 3, 2017 as that university's first female and first Hispanic president. She is omitted from the university's official past-chancellors list.

leaders.notes: Title in effect: Chancellor. An external hire: UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt selected Rogerson in May 2016 after an eight-month national search that produced three finalists, and he took office September 1, 2016 as the university's tenth chancellor, with an investiture on May 11, 2017. A native of Scotland with a doctorate in protozoan ecology, he had previously held posts at Marshall University and Fresno State. Amid enrollment decline and budget cuts he announced on August 30, 2019 that he would step down effective September 1, 2019, saying it would be best for him to step aside.

leaders.priorTitle: Interim Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost
leaders.priorInstitution: University of Arkansas at Little Rock (internal appointment)
leaders.notes: Title in effect: Chancellor; sitting incumbent, so endYear is null. A fully internal appointment: Drale joined UALR in 2006 as associate dean of the College of Professional Studies after nearly 20 years at Missouri State University, became associate vice chancellor for academic affairs in 2011, and was serving as interim executive vice chancellor and provost from October 2018 when UA System President Donald R. Bobbitt named her acting chancellor on September 4-5, 2019 after Andrew Rogerson's forced resignation; the UA Board of Trustees unanimously made the appointment permanent on September 12, 2019. She holds BA, MA and PhD degrees from UC San Diego. She told the UA Board of Trustees in May 2026 (reported May 21-22, 2026) that she will retire effective June 30, 2027, at the end of the 2026-27 academic year, saying "It's just time for me" after about 40 years in higher education, and wanting to finish the university's centennial year and its $250 million Centennial Campaign. UA System President Jay B. Silveria announced the advisory chancellor search committee on July 16, 2026 (reported by the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette on July 23, 2026), chaired by UALR vice provost for research and graduate dean Brian Berry and including UA trustee Ashley Caldwell and Little Rock city director Dean Kumpuris; the committee will work with a search firm and the position is to be advertised beginning early in the fall 2026 semester, with Silveria aiming to identify a successor before Drale departs.
